opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we went back and forth on quite a bit internally.

When we started out, the natural instinct, coming from the quantum computing world, was to go cold. We actually built early prototypes using superconducting circuits, Josephson junctions, operating at cryogenic temperatures. And there are real advantages there. You get very clean, well-characterized noise. You have lower thermal noise floors, so you have a lot of control over exactly how much stochasticity you're injecting into the system. And superconducting elements give you these really nice nonlinearities that are great for engineering interesting energy landscapes.

But the whole point of what we're doing is to use noise as a resource rather than fight it. If you take that seriously, cooling everything down to millikelvin and then carefully reintroducing noise starts to look a bit backwards. You're spending enormous energy on refrigeration to suppress the very thing you want to harness. So there's a philosophical tension there.

Then there's the practical side. Cryogenics doesn't scale the way you want for mass deployment. Dilution refrigerators are expensive, bulky, and slow to iterate on. If your goal is to put probabilistic computing into data centers, and eventually at the edge, you need something that runs at room temperature on a standard CMOS process. That's where the economics and the ecosystem are. You inherit decades of fabrication know-how, packaging, and supply chain.

So the way we weigh it: cryogenic superconducting systems were a fantastic testbed for physics and proving out the principles. You can study the thermodynamics very cleanly. But for the product, room-temperature silicon wins. The challenge then becomes engineering. Thermal noise at room temperature is much larger, so you need to design circuits where the signal-to-noise ratio sits in the right regime, where fluctuations do useful sampling work instead of washing everything out. You also have to deal with device mismatch and variability across the chip, which you'd otherwise want to calibrate away.

What's interesting is that a lot of that variability is something a learning system can absorb. If the hardware is trained in the loop, it can adapt to its own imperfections. So instead of demanding perfect, deterministic components, you co-design the algorithm with the physics of the chip. That's the bet: go where the scale is, embrace the noise of the real world at three hundred kelvin, and let the learning paradigm make up for the lack of pristine control you'd have in a fridge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses refrigeration costs and the benefits of room-temperature silicon, but does not state that the computer itself consumes less energy at lower temperatures when thermal-bath maintenance is excluded.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and it's really the question that defines our whole design philosophy at Extropic. So the short answer is: we're betting on room temperature, and we think that's actually the whole point.

Let me explain why. The whole premise of thermodynamic computing is that you're not fighting noise, you're using it. A conventional digital computer spends enormous amounts of energy keeping every bit deterministic, pinning it to zero or one against thermal fluctuations. A superconducting quantum computer goes even further in that direction. You cool everything down to tens of millikelvin precisely so that thermal noise doesn't destroy the delicate coherent state you're trying to maintain. That's a very expensive way to compute, both in capital cost for the dilution fridges and in the sheer energy overhead of refrigeration, which can be orders of magnitude larger than the energy of the computation itself.

Our approach flips that. We want the noise. The native computational primitive on our chips is essentially a stochastic sample. The physics of the device is doing the random number generation and the probabilistic inference for you, for free, because the thermal bath is driving the dynamics. So if you take that philosophy seriously, cryogenic operation is almost self-defeating. If you cool the chip down, you're suppressing the very resource you're trying to harness, and you're paying a huge energy tax to do it.

Now, to be fair, early on we did explore superconducting implementations, because there's a historical path through Josephson junction physics where a lot of this stochastic circuit theory originated. And at cryogenic temperatures you get beautifully clean, low-dissipation devices where you can characterize the noise very precisely. That's great for a scientific demonstration. But it doesn't scale into something you'd actually deploy in a data center next to a GPU.

So the engineering trade-off we made is to go to silicon, standard CMOS processes, operating at room temperature. The noise there is messier, it's a mix of thermal noise, shot noise, flicker noise, and you have to design your circuits so that the statistics of what you're sampling from are well characterized and controllable despite that. That's the hard part. But the payoff is that you get something manufacturable at existing fabs, something that integrates with conventional digital control logic, and something whose energy per sample can genuinely be thousands of times lower than doing the equivalent sampling on a GPU, because you're not emulating randomness with deterministic arithmetic, you're just letting physics do it.

So I'd frame it this way. Cryogenics buys you precision and low dissipation, but at the cost of accessibility and total system energy. Room temperature costs you some precision and forces you to be very clever about circuit design and calibration, but it's the only path where the thermodynamic advantage actually survives contact with the real world. For us, the whole thesis is that intelligence at scale is fundamentally a problem of sampling and inference under uncertainty, and the most efficient machine for that is one that lives in the same thermal regime as the world it's modeling. So room temperature isn't a compromise. It's the bet.

r001.rationale: The response says cryogenic devices can have low dissipation, but it does not state that a thermodynamic computer consumes less energy at lower temperatures when refrigeration costs are excluded.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to look at the energy budget of the whole system. Cooling reduces the thermal energy scale, so you can potentially operate with smaller switching energies, but you have to pay for refrigeration. A lower energy per operation on the chip doesn’t automatically translate into a more efficient machine.

And for thermodynamic computing, thermal fluctuations are part of the computational resource. The objective isn’t simply to get rid of noise; it’s to engineer the dynamics so that the noise helps you sample the distribution you care about. You can, in principle, do that at different temperatures by choosing the relevant energy scales appropriately.

Room-temperature operation is attractive because it simplifies deployment and integration. Cryogenic operation becomes compelling if it gives you enough of an advantage in control, speed, or energy per useful sample to outweigh the cooling overhead. So I’d weigh them at the system level, for a particular workload, rather than treating colder as inherently better.

r001.rationale: It says cooling can enable smaller switching energies and that energy per operation on the chip can be lower, while treating refrigeration as a separate overhead.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the right way to weigh it is at the system level. Cooling lowers the thermal energy scale, so you can potentially do the computation with less energy on the chip. But the refrigerator has a cost, and you have to include getting signals in and out. A low energy per operation doesn’t automatically mean a low energy bill.

For a thermodynamic computer, noise is also part of the computational resource. You’re engineering the relationship between fluctuations, coupling strengths, and the dynamics you want to sample. Room-temperature operation is attractive because it makes deployment and integration much simpler, provided you can control those dynamics well enough.

So I wouldn’t say colder is inherently better. I’d compare useful samples per second, their quality, and the total wall-plug energy required to produce them. Cryogenics has to earn its place through an advantage in that complete picture.
